pergunta: What could a fast armored car, with a small gun and a thin floor, do in a war of tanks?
resumo: M8 Greyhound, the FEB's armored car in Italy: specs, strengths and weak points, and the reconnaissance squadron at Montese. A source for every figure.
abertura: The M8 was a six-wheeled armored car, built by Ford, with a 37 mm gun in an open turret. In the US Army, it was the vehicle of the reconnaissance squadrons. Greyhound, after the racing dog, was the name the British gave it.

For Brazil, it has a place apart: it was the armored car of the 1st Reconnaissance Squadron of the Brazilian Expeditionary Force, the only Brazilian unit to use armor in the Second World War, according to the magazine of the Army's Armor Instruction Center.

paragrafos: The American manual of 1943 defines the purpose in one line: to give high-speed mobility, defensive fire and crew protection for reconnaissance. The M8 went ahead to see, come back and report. It was not a fighting piece.

Curiously, it was born for something else. The design began as a light wheeled tank destroyer, with the 37 mm gun. By the time it was ready, in 1942, that gun was no longer seen as an effective anti-tank weapon, and the vehicle was standardized as an armored reconnaissance car.
The road. At about 90 km/h on firm going, the M8 was much faster than any tank. The Lewis Army Museum sums it up: it ran well on a hard surface and badly on everything else.

The mechanics. The same museum describes it as mechanically sound, and Military Vehicles magazine, as generally more reliable than tracked vehicles of the same size. For a unit that lives far from the workshop, that counts.
The floor. With a quarter of an inch of plate underneath, the M8 was very vulnerable to mines, and the Germans used minefields on a large scale. The crews lined the floor with sandbags.

The open turret, which left the crew exposed to whatever came from above, and the gun. According to Steven Zaloga, as cited by the English Wikipedia, the 37 mm was not effective against the frontal armor of German tanks; it was good against light vehicles and infantry.

And the terrain. Off road, above all in mud and snow, mobility was poor, according to Nicholas Moran, as cited by the English Wikipedia, and worse than that of tracked and half-tracked vehicles, according to J. Rickard.

The 1st Reconnaissance Squadron of the Brazilian division received the American equipment once it was in Italy. Each reconnaissance platoon had three patrols, and each patrol, one M8 and two jeeps. In the winter of 1944 to 1945, with the front stalled in the Apennines, the squadron was used practically as a rifle company; only from Montese on did it return to reconnaissance.

The two weak points on this page show up in the Brazilian record. According to Captain Plínio Pitaluga, the squadron commander, one M8 was put out of action by a German anti-tank mine during a reconnaissance, in the phase that runs from Montese to the Panaro river. On 28 April 1945, at Felegara, another was set on fire by a rocket-launcher projectile; the crew got out unharmed.
At Collecchio, on 26 and 27 April, it was the squadron that made the first contact with the vanguard of the German 148th Division, and the 37 mm gun answered the fire of enemy reconnaissance cars.

batalhas.texto: According to the English Wikipedia, the Brazilian infantry advanced on 14 April 1945 with M8 armored cars and Sherman tanks. The advance, fast and with armor, led the German command to treat Montese as a possible real Allied objective, and the FEB received around two thirds of the sector's artillery.

Captain Pitaluga's Reconnaissance Squadron, the unit that used the M8 in the FEB, opens the contact with the German column. Behind it come the infantry regiments, and on 29 April 1945 the German 148th Infantry Division surrenders.

veredito: On the board, the M8 is the piece that travels far and does not trade. Its worth lies in what it sees, not in what it destroys: getting there first, finding the enemy, measuring and coming back.

Used that way, it delivered. Put to fight, it was exposed at its weakest: the floor, the open turret, the small gun. The line attributed to Pitaluga by the English Wikipedia points the same way: the M8 is for reconnaissance, not for heavy combat.

mitos.circula: Greyhound was the American name for the vehicle.
mitos.registro: The name is British. The American manual of 1943 calls it simply the light armored car M8. The reason for the name differs: the speed, according to Military Vehicles magazine; the series of dog names the British were already giving to American armored cars, according to the English Wikipedia.

mitos.circula: 11,000 or 12,000 of the M8 were built.
mitos.registro: There were 8,523. The larger number adds in the M20, the turretless variant, with about 3,790.

mitos.circula: The Germans called the M8 cars Patton's ghosts, they were so quiet.
mitos.registro: The story is repeated on many pages, always with no German document and no record from Patton's army. The best source found already gives it as an allegation.

mitos.circula: The M8 was a tank destroyer that did not work out.
mitos.registro: It is a half-truth. The design began as a light tank destroyer, but the vehicle was already standardized in 1942 as an armored reconnaissance car, and that is what the manual defines it for.

perguntas.p: How many M8 Greyhound cars were built?
perguntas.r: 8,523, by Ford, from March 1943 on. The totals of 11,000 or 12,000 add in the M20 variant, without a turret.

perguntas.p: What gun did the M8 Greyhound carry?
perguntas.r: A 37 mm M6 gun, in an open, hand-traversed turret, with 80 rounds. It was good against light vehicles and infantry, not against the front of German tanks.

perguntas.p: Did the FEB use armor in Italy?
perguntas.r: Yes: the M8, in the 1st Reconnaissance Squadron. There were 15 on establishment, with 13 in use, in the sources linked to the Army, and 13 in the Portuguese Wikipedia.

perguntas.p: Why is the M8 called Greyhound?
perguntas.r: The name was given by the British. The reason differs with the source: the vehicle's speed, or the series of dog names they gave to American armored cars.
